case_name: Dwarkadas Marfatia And Sons v Board Of Trustees Of The Port Of Bombay
respondent:
Board Of Trustees Of The Port Of Bombay
Supreme Court of India

27 April 1989
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 2036 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 19.11.1986 of the Bombay High Court in W.P. No. 710of 1984
The Judgment was delivered by: Sabyasachi Mukharji, J.
1.  This is an appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated 19th November, 1986 of the learned Single Judge of the Bombay High Court. In this appeal this Court has been asked to examine the frontiers of judicial review of the action of a statutory authority, i.e. the Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay, in evicting its tenant and granting the land in question to another tenant. However, in order to appreciate the controversy it is necessary to have a conspectus of the facts involved.
2.  The respondent Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay is a statutory authority. Vast areas of South Bombay which are completely tenanted are owned by the respondent. Being
facts: The respondent Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay is a statutory authority.

Between about 1906 and 1932, one Jhunjhunwala was the lessee of plot No. 6 (which adjoins plot 5B which is the suit plot) and a building was existing on plot No. 6 which was tenanted to M/s Bombay Bharat & Swadeshi Rice Mills.
Since about 1932, the appellant had been the lessee of the respondent in respect of part of the original plot No. 4 (now plot 5B) which adjoins plot No. 6 of the suit plot measuring 113.4 sq. mts.
In or about 1933-34, with a view to acquire the suit plot and using the same for the rice mill/dust room, M/s Bombay Bharat & Swadeshi Rice Mills took over the appellant.
The dust room structure was constructed on the suit plot.
It was stated that the respondent's inspectors had regularly visited the premises in question but had never objected to the user of the rice mill/dust room.
In December'57, the Town Planning Scheme No. 1 in Bombay City came into force.
The original plot No. 4 was reconstituted into final plot No. 5 but continued to belong to the respondent.
From 1957-72, the respondent, it is asserted, continued the tenancies of the appellant and its associate firms.
In or about 1963, however, the respondent applied for and got final plot No. 5 sub-divided into final plot 5A (659 sq. mts.) and final plot 5B (650 sq. mts.).

It is the case of the appellant that in 1970-71, the respondent arbitrarily agreed to let the entire plot 5B including the portion which had been let to and in the possession of the appellant since 1933 to M/s Dhanji Mavji.
The appellant offered to develop final plot 5B jointly with Dhanji Mavji in 1972-76.
In or about October 1977, the respondent issued one month's notice to the appellant to terminate the tenancy.
In December, 1977 the respondent filed suits Nos. 447 & 603/77 against the appellant in the Court of Small Causes, Bombay.
issues: Whether the action of the respondent in evicting the appellant and granting the premises in question to M/s Dhanji Mavji was proper and right.
Whether the eviction of the appellant was necessary in public interest.

Whether the decision of the Port Trust to allot the entire plot to M/s Dhanji Mavji to the exclusion of the appellant (although the appellant was thereof for the past 40 years) was an arbitrary and discriminatory departure from the established policy of the Port Trust.
petitioner_arguments: The action of the respondent in terminating the appellant's contractual tenancy had a public law character attached to it and was accordingly subject to judicial review.

Every action of the respondent which was 'State' within Art. 12 of the Constitution, whether it be in the field of contract, or any other field, was subject to Art. 14 of the Constitution and must be reasonable and taken only upon lawful and relevant grounds of public interest.
The eviction of the appellant was not necessary in public interest.

The decision of the Port Trust to allot the entire plot to M/s Dhanji Mavji to the exclusion of the appellant (although the appellant was thereof for the past 40 years) was an arbitrary and discriminatory departure from the established policy of the Port Trust.
respondent_arguments: The respondent had a statutory obligation to grant the entire plot to the person who occupied the major portion thereof.
The decision of the Port Trust to allot the entire plot to M/s Dhanji Mavji was in accordance with the established policy of the Port Trust.
court_reasoning: In our opinion, the High Court was right on this aspect and in any event u/art. 227 of the Constitution the High Court could not have gone into this question.
We, in an appeal u/art. 136 of the Constitution cannot re-appraise that question.

It appears that the eviction of the appellant was only in pursuance of a policy of the Port Trust to let out a reconstituted plot to the person who occupied the major portion and who could use it for development.
holding: The action of the respondent in evicting the appellant and granting the premises in question to M/s Dhanji Mavji was proper and right.
The eviction of the appellant was necessary in public interest.
The decision of the Port Trust to allot the entire plot to M/s Dhanji Mavji was not arbitrary and discriminatory.
